PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 82 — Lesson 106: Osteoporosis & Fracture Prevention

FNP-level goal: Identify patients at elevated fracture risk, apply screening and diagnostic testing appropriately, look for secondary causes, build a fall- and fracture-prevention plan, and manage/monitor therapy with patient-specific safety and referral decisions.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish screening, diagnosis, and treatment assessment in osteoporosis and fragility-fracture prevention.
  • Recognize risk factors and secondary causes that require targeted evaluation rather than a one-size-fits-all screening approach.
  • Explain the role of DXA, T-scores, fracture-risk estimation, and vertebral/fragility fracture history in clinical context.
  • Integrate nutrition, activity, resistance/balance training, fall prevention, medication review, and treatment adherence into a realistic plan.
  • Recognize acute fracture, neurologic compromise, severe pain, medication complications, and complex bone disease that need urgent or specialty care.

Part 1 — The Goal Is Preventing the Next Fracture

Osteoporosis is a skeletal disorder marked by reduced bone strength and increased fracture risk. It is often silent until a fragility fracture occurs. Hip, vertebral, wrist, humerus, and other low-trauma fractures can lead to pain, loss of independence, disability, future fractures, and mortality. The FNP should treat a fragility fracture as a sentinel event: ask why it occurred, assess risk, protect immediate function, and make sure bone-health follow-up is not lost after the acute injury visit.

Screening guidance differs from diagnostic evaluation. For adults without known osteoporosis or fragility fracture, the USPSTF recommends screening women 65 years or older and postmenopausal women younger than 65 years at increased risk. Evidence remains insufficient to make a population-wide screening recommendation for men, so clinical judgment and risk assessment remain essential. These screening recommendations do not substitute for evaluation of a fragility fracture, secondary osteoporosis, or medication-associated bone loss.

Part 2 — Risk Assessment and Secondary Causes

Ask about prior low-trauma fracture, parental hip fracture, falls, low body weight, menopause/hypogonadism context, tobacco, alcohol, mobility, nutrition, calcium/vitamin D intake, eating disorder, malabsorption, inflammatory disease, CKD, liver disease, endocrine disease, cancer treatment, transplant, and long-term or recurrent glucocorticoid exposure. Review medication contributors such as glucocorticoids, aromatase inhibitors, androgen-deprivation therapy, antiseizure medications, proton-pump inhibitors in context, and others. Evaluate based on patient history rather than sending every test to every patient.

Secondary causes may include hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin-D deficiency, renal disease, malabsorption/celiac disease, hypogonadism, hematologic disease, inflammatory disease, medication exposure, and cancer-related bone disease. Unexpected severity, young age, recurrent fractures, abnormal calcium/renal findings, unexplained weight loss, or multiple endocrine symptoms lower the threshold for targeted laboratory evaluation and specialty collaboration.

Part 3 — DXA, T-Scores and Fracture Risk

DXA measures bone mineral density, commonly at hip and lumbar spine. A T-score compares the result with a young-adult reference population; it is useful but does not capture every determinant of fracture risk. Fracture-risk tools can integrate age, prior fracture, glucocorticoid exposure, smoking, alcohol, body size, and other factors, but results must be interpreted with clinical judgment. A person with a fragility fracture may be at high risk even when the number alone does not tell the whole story.

Do not reduce the conversation to “osteopenia versus osteoporosis.” Ask: Has the patient fractured? What is their fall risk? Is bone loss likely secondary? Is the result technically reliable? Will a test change therapy or monitoring? Is the patient able to obtain and adhere to the plan?

Part 4 — Falls Prevention Is Fracture Prevention

Fracture prevention requires more than calcium advice. Assess prior falls, fear of falling, gait/balance, vision/hearing, neuropathy, orthostasis, footwear, assistive devices, home hazards, alcohol/substance use, cognition, and sedating/hypotensive medications. Strength, balance, resistance, and weight-bearing activity should be individualized to fracture risk, pain, mobility, and fall risk. In a frail patient, “start intense exercise” can be unsafe; physical therapy, supervised programs, home modifications, and caregiver involvement may be needed.

Nutrition counseling should be practical. Review dietary intake, supplements, renal disease, hypercalcemia history, constipation, pill burden, affordability, and eating habits. Avoid implying that supplements alone reverse established high fracture risk. The goal is a sustainable total prevention plan.

Part 5 — Medication Selection and Monitoring

Pharmacologic treatment is individualized by fracture history, bone density/risk assessment, kidney function, GI/esophageal issues, calcium/vitamin-D status, dental/oral health context, pregnancy potential where relevant, cancer history, treatment access, and patient preference. Antiresorptive and anabolic options have different indications, routes, adverse effects, sequencing, and discontinuation considerations. The FNP must know what question the drug is answering, how it will be monitored, and who owns the plan.

Before and during therapy, reconcile medications, confirm adherence and administration technique, review new dental procedures or jaw symptoms as clinically relevant, ask about new thigh/groin pain or other concerning symptoms, monitor indicated labs/renal function, and plan reassessment rather than indefinite therapy without review. Some therapies require transition planning when stopped; do not abruptly discontinue or delay a scheduled agent without understanding the consequence and coordinating with the prescriber/specialist.

Part 6 — Urgent Care and Referral

New severe back pain with height loss or kyphosis can represent vertebral compression fracture and deserves timely assessment. Hip pain or inability to bear weight after a fall, new neurologic symptoms, suspected pathologic fracture, severe uncontrolled pain, or possible spinal cord compromise requires urgent or emergency evaluation. Refer or collaborate with endocrinology, rheumatology, nephrology, oncology, orthopedics, fracture liaison services, physical therapy, and geriatrics when secondary disease, CKD-mineral/bone disorder, recurrent fractures, complex therapy selection, or major functional risk is present.

Clinical Case

A 67-year-old postmenopausal woman has a wrist fracture after falling from standing height. She has had two falls this year, uses a chronic glucocorticoid for inflammatory disease, and has not had a bone-health evaluation.

FNP reasoning: this is a fragility-fracture and secondary-risk evaluation, not merely a cast follow-up. Assess acute recovery and falls, review glucocorticoid exposure and potential secondary contributors, arrange appropriate bone-density/fracture-risk evaluation, address medications and home safety, and establish a coordinated treatment and monitoring plan. The goal is preventing the next fracture, especially a hip or vertebral fracture.

FNP Osteoporosis Framework

  1. Identify the fracture-risk context: age, menopausal/hormonal status, prior fracture, falls, medications, disease, and lifestyle.
  2. Separate screening from diagnosis: use current screening guidance but evaluate fragility fracture/secondary causes directly.
  3. Interpret DXA and risk in context: numbers, fracture history, reliability, fall risk, and whether results change management.
  4. Prevent falls and bone loss: activity/balance, nutrition, medication review, vision/home safety, tobacco/alcohol support, and access.
  5. Make therapy safe: indication, administration, organ function, adverse effects, adherence, reassessment, and transition plan.

High-Yield Summary

Fragility fracture: is a sentinel event requiring bone-health and fall-risk follow-up.
Screening: includes women 65+ and younger postmenopausal women at increased risk; men require individualized clinical judgment under USPSTF guidance.
DXA: informs risk but does not replace fracture history, secondary-cause evaluation, or functional assessment.
Fall prevention: is a core fracture-prevention intervention.
Therapy: must be matched to risk, organs/comorbidities, administration feasibility, monitoring, and discontinuation plan.
FNP standard: prevent the next fracture by integrating bone, fall, medication, function, and access care.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Osteoporosis screening/diagnosis, DXA interpretation, laboratory evaluation, pharmacotherapy, fracture management, referral, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, local policy, collaboration/scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
